text:
The fastest way to kill a Platform Engineering initiative:

Spend 6 months building an Internal Developer Portal nobody asked for.

Automate their top 3 Slack tickets instead: preview DBs, secrets, DNS.

What's the one thing your devs keep asking for?

Enterprise Azure migrations don't stall on Kubernetes or the database.

They stall on subscription governance in week one.

Ship the landing zone guardrails in Terraform before a single service goes live.

What blew up the timeline on your last migration?

Enterprise RAG rarely fails on the vector DB or the embedding model.

It fails on chunk boundaries and metadata filtering.

No document hierarchy, no access scopes, and the LLM serves you garbage with total confidence.

How are you chunking yours?

From December 2026, Australian law says you must show how an automated decision was made.

A PDF policy won't survive an OAIC audit.

You need a tamper-evident log at the code layer.

Is your AI actually audit-ready, or does it just look compliant?

I've watched technically 'perfect' architectures die in enterprise rollouts.

Not because the design was wrong.

Because nobody on the team wanted to use it.

A simple system with 100% buy-in wins every time. Where have you seen this play out?

Non-profit IT taught me more about security than any enterprise budget did.

With no money, you can't buy your way out of a threat.

Strict Entra ID MFA and domain lockdown protect vulnerable helplines for $0 in extra tooling.

Your highest-ROI security control?

Early on, you measure yourself by how much code you write.

Later, by how much complexity you kept out of production.

The best PRs I review now delete more than they add.

When did that shift click for you?

A Terraform pattern that shrinks your blast radius to near zero:

Split state by how often things change, not by environment.

Landing zones (yearly) ≠ AKS (monthly) ≠ app deploys (daily).

Bicep or Terraform for you in 2026?

Developer velocity isn't how fast your team types code.

It's how little stands between `git push` and verified-in-production, with zero fear of breaking the build.

If QA sign-off takes 3 weeks, that's not CI/CD. It's a queue.

What's your lead time?

Treat LLM tool calling like distributed systems RPC, or it bites you in production:

1. Client idempotency keys
2. Strict Zod/Pydantic validation
3. Deterministic fallbacks when the model hallucinates args

Never trust raw LLM JSON. What's burned you here?

The first rule when I architected ADM Guard: zero PII by design.

If a payload carries a name, email, or tax ID, the gateway rejects it with HTTP 422 before anything is stored.

You can't leak data you never hold.

Would you trust this boundary?

8+ years shipping enterprise systems taught me one golden rule:

Design for the failure mode first.

If you can't say what happens when a downstream call returns 504 or the network partitions, the design isn't done.

What failure mode do most teams ignore?

The highest-leverage IT work in a non-profit isn't a shiny new SaaS.

It's killing shadow IT, closing phishing vectors, and giving volunteers tools that simply never crash.

Boring reliability beats features here.

Most underrated 'boring' fix you've shipped?

Running enterprise consulting and building a startup at once comes down to one thing:

Zero context-switching inside a focus block.

Consulting builds discipline. The startup demands speed. Together they sharpen you.

How do you protect deep work?
